## Executive summary

Write a one-paragraph abstract summarizing what you did and your findings. It need not be comprehensive; try to highlight the most important or interesting outcomes.

When looking at whether comfort levels and course counts, we failed to find correlation. This was also the case when considering if students with interest in Lab vs Industry positions favored either Python or R. \[smth about question 3\]. The greatest obstacle in this research was the small sample size, which made rejecting null hypothesis challenging.

## Data description

Write a brief description of the dataset. Your description should cover how data were obtained, sample characteristics, and measurements taken. It does not need to be exhaustive, but sufficiently detailed to convey a clear high-level understanding of the dataset. You can utilize bullet points or tables if you feel it would help improve clarity.

The data was obtained from the PSTAT197A course survey, which was sent out to students at the beginning of the 2026 fall quarter. The survey was anonymized and consisted of two parts: a background survey and an interest survey. The background survey collected information on students' comfort levels with programming, mathematics, and statistics, as well as the number of upper division courses they had taken. The interest survey gathered data on students' preferred areas of study within data science, their programming language preferences, and their career track orientation (Industry-only vs. Lab-inclined). Given that students were given the option to have their responses included in the analysis, the sample consisted of 51 responses for the background survey and 49 responses for the interest survey.

One important characteristic is that the sample size is small, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, the survey responses are self-reported, which may introduce bias or inaccuracies in the data. Such as with proficiency, where students may overestimate or underestimate their abilities.

The data is that it includes both categorical and discrete numerical variables. Comfort levels are measured on a 1-5 scale, while the number of upper division courses is a categorical variable with three levels (3-5, 6-8, 9+). Programming language preference is a categorical variable with three levels (Python, R, No preference), and career track orientation is a binary variable (Industry-only vs. Lab-inclined).

## Questions of interest

Indicate the questions your analysis addresses. These should map one-to-one to your findings. Don't include questions you didn't answer or questions you started with and refined later. If you would rather frame them as goals or tasks rather than questions that is okay; just modify the header appropriately. However you frame what you've done, you may only have two or three items; that is fine. Provide an itemized or numbered list so that the reader can easily identify your objectives.

For example:

> We explored how students’ academic experiences and personal interests relate to their experiences and future goals in data science. Specifically, we investigated the connection between coursework and technical confidence, the relationship between programming preferences and career plans, and the possibility of identifying common patterns in students’ areas of interest. These questions guided our analysis:
>
> 1.  *Is coursework preparation associated with students' self reported comfort levels with technical skills?*
> 2.  *Is programming language preference associated with students' career track orientation (industry-only vs lab-inclined)?*
> 3.  *Are there underlying patterns in students' data science interests that reveal distinct groups of students?*

## Useful tips (remove this section)

Due to the visual editor, most common needs for authoring can be met using menu items in the RStudio IDE. For a comprehensive guide to Quarto, see the [documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/); consult the documentation for anything you can't sort out in the IDE.

### Code chunks

Insert code chunks using the *Insert* drop-down menu or `ctrl + alt + I` . By default in this document, codes will not be shown but results will. If you want to change this behavior, add the chunk option `echo: true` as below.

```{r}
#| echo: true
my_df <- tibble(animal = c('snake', 'gecko'),
                threatening = c(TRUE, FALSE))

my_df
```

Code chunks will be executed in order when the document is rendered, so packages should be loaded at the very beginning of the document

### Rendering tables in markdown

Several functions exist for converting dataframes to markdown tables for nice display. A simple one from the `knitr` package is `knitr::kable()` .

```{r}
my_df %>% knitr::kable()
```

### Figures

To include any figures not generated by code chunks, use *Insert \> Figure / Image* or `![CAPTION](path/file.ext)` .

Most of the time code chunks producing plots will render fine. However, to adjust sizing or alignment, use the chunk options `fig-width` and `fig-height` . Captions can be added with `fig-cap` .

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: left
#| fig-cap: A terrible plot.

my_df %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = animal, y = threatening)) + 
  geom_col()
```

### Links

To include any hyperlinks, use `[display text](url)` .
